# Results — Study 397 (Hurst-Regime)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim: the
**Hurst exponent** of a price series tells you whether it is **trending** (H > 0.5 ⇒
trend-follow) or **mean-reverting** (H < 0.5 ⇒ fade), so a rolling-Hurst-gated switch between
the two styles should beat either style alone. We estimate a trailing **R/S** Hurst on real
markets (SPY headline + QQQ/GLD/TLT/EFA), build the trend / revert / Hurst-gated books on a
1-day execution lag net of one-way costs, and test whether the gate adds anything a shuffled
regime label wouldn't. Offline core + synthetic control are deterministic; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — SPY (headline) + QQQ, GLD, TLT, EFA (public, no key) |
| Window (SPY) | 1995-01-03 → 2026-06-18 (**7,918** trading days; **31.5** years) |
| Hurst estimator | trailing **R/S** rescaled-range over a **252-day** window, pure-trailing (no look-ahead) |
| Styles switched | trend = sign of trailing 63-day return; revert = −sign of trailing 5-day return |
| Gate | H > 0.5 ⇒ trend, H < 0.5 ⇒ revert, H undefined ⇒ flat |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag; **1 bp** one-way cost × turnover |
| As-of | 2026-06-22 (last bar 2026-06-18; no partial bar) |

> **The first surprise is in the estimator, not the strategy.** SPY's rolling 252-day R/S
> Hurst sits at **mean 0.552, median 0.553, std 0.050**, and **never leaves [0.36, 0.695]** —
> it is **above 0.5 on 84%** of the days the gate can act on. So the "switch to mean-reversion"
> the claim promises almost never fires: the gate is a trend-follower wearing a regime costume. This is
> the well-known small-sample **upward bias** of R/S on ~1-year windows (Hurst 1951; Lo 1991),
> and it already guts the premise before any P&L is measured.

## The four books — the gate is worse than holding *and* worse than the best static style

1-day entry lag; 1 bp one-way cost × turnover. Sharpe is annualised; all books are run at the
same ~19% annual vol, so Sharpe is the apples-to-apples comparison.

| book | Sharpe | ann. mean | ann. vol |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **buy & hold** | **+0.66** | +12.4% | 19.0% |
| always-trend | +0.10 | +1.9% | 19.0% |
| always-revert | +0.25 | +4.8% | 19.0% |
| **Hurst-gated switch** | **+0.17** | +3.2% | 18.9% |

The punchline is brutal in one line: the **Hurst-gated book (+0.17) loses to the best static
style (always-revert, +0.25) and is crushed by simply holding SPY (+0.66).** Conditioning the
style on the Hurst exponent does not help — it *hurts*.

## The decisive test — does the gate beat the best static style, or a shuffled label?

| comparison | Sharpe difference | 95% CI (block bootstrap) | p-value |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| gated − best static (revert) | **−0.085** | [−0.549, +0.364] | p(diff ≤ 0) = **0.654** |
| gated − buy & hold | **−0.486** | — | p(diff ≤ 0) = **0.979** |
| paired daily *t* (gated − best static) | **−0.322** | — | — |
| placebo: block-shuffle the regime label | real edge −0.085 vs placebo mean −0.160 | — | p = **0.215** |

Read it carefully. The gate's Sharpe edge over the best static style is **negative** (−0.09)
with a confidence interval that straddles zero and is **more likely negative than positive**
(p = 0.65). The paired daily *t* is **−0.32** — nowhere near the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar, and the
**wrong sign**. The **placebo** is the cleanest verdict of all: when we block-shuffle the
regime label — breaking any real H→style link while keeping the same style mix — the shuffled
gate does *about as well* (its mean edge is even slightly more negative), and a shuffle matches
or beats the real Hurst gate **22%** of the time. **The Hurst path carries no usable
regime-timing information.**

## Every market, same story

| market | H mean | share H>0.5 | gated | best static | buy & hold |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 0.552 | 84% | +0.17 | +0.25 | **+0.66** |
| QQQ | 0.558 | 87% | +0.29 | +0.13 | **+0.52** |
| GLD | 0.592 | 97% | +0.32 | +0.32 | **+0.64** |
| TLT | 0.564 | 86% | +0.19 | +0.22 | **+0.33** |
| EFA | 0.564 | 91% | −0.03 | +0.12 | **+0.41** |

In **5 of 5** markets the gated book is beaten by buy-and-hold; it beats the best static style
in **one** (QQQ, by a noisy +0.16) and loses or ties in the other four. Every market shows the
same R/S bias (H pinned in the high-0.5s, 84–97% of valid days "trending"), so the gate is a
trend-follower everywhere — and trend-following SPY-like tapes underperforms holding them.

## Robustness — no Hurst window rescues it

| Hurst window | gated Sharpe | best static | buy & hold |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 126 days | +0.22 | +0.25 | +0.66 |
| **252 days** (headline) | +0.17 | +0.25 | +0.66 |
| 504 days | +0.06 | +0.25 | +0.66 |

The *best* window (126) gets the gate to +0.22 — still well under both the best static style
(+0.25) and a third of buy-and-hold. There is no window at which the Hurst gate becomes a
reason to switch styles, let alone to allocate capital.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is faithful; the real tape just has no edge

**Control 1 — the estimator recovers a planted Hurst.** On fractional-Gaussian paths with a
*known* H, the R/S estimator lands on it (the mild low-H bias is the documented small-sample
R/S bias, the very thing that pins real-tape H above 0.5):

| planted H | R/S estimate |
|---|--:|
| 0.30 | 0.384 |
| 0.50 | 0.550 |
| 0.70 | 0.717 |

**Control 2 — the gate's power test.** On a deterministic path whose regime *alternates* in
blocks, with a planted-edge knob (`edge` = the true Hurst separation between regimes):

| planted edge | gated Sharpe | trend | revert | gated − best static | p(boot) | p(placebo) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (both regimes random walk) | −0.23 | −0.22 | −0.33 | **−0.007** | 0.477 | 0.434 |
| **1.00** (clean H separation) | +0.42 | −0.07 | −0.74 | **+0.486** | **0.044** | **0.000** |

With **no** real regime structure (`edge = 0`) the gate does **not** manufacture an edge
(difference ≈ 0, both nulls ≈ 0.45). With a **strong, clean** regime separation (`edge = 1`)
the Hurst gate **lights up** — it beats both static styles, the bootstrap p drops to 0.044 and
the placebo p to 0.000. The control proves the harness *can* detect a real Hurst-regime edge
when one exists; the real tape's −0.09 / p = 0.65 / placebo p = 0.22 is exactly what an
**absent** edge looks like through a faithful machine.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The Hurst exponent does **not** forecast which style will pay. On SPY the
  gate's daily edge over the best static style is **−0.32 t** (wrong sign, far below *t* ≥ 2),
  the bootstrap CI straddles zero (p = 0.65), and the **placebo says a shuffled regime label
  does just as well (p = 0.22)** — the H path adds nothing. The synthetic control confirms this
  is a true null, not a power failure.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Beyond *no edge over the static styles*, the gated book is
  **−0.49 Sharpe worse than simply holding SPY** (p = 0.98) in every market tested. It is a
  worse version of buy-and-hold dressed as market timing. Costs are tiny; the problem is that
  the signal is empty.
- **Free lunch? — BUSTED.** The romance — "let the math of the series tell you when to trend
  and when to fade" — runs aground on two facts: trailing R/S Hurst on real markets is **pinned
  above 0.5** (so the switch barely switches), and even where it does switch it carries **no
  forecasting power**. The Hurst exponent is a real, well-defined object; reading regime *trades*
  off it is a category error.
